edition.deck: COP31 ends without a central deal as governments clash over fossil fuels and finance; a Russian ship is hit in Libya, and violence spreads across West Bank villages.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and genuinely new updates, while retaining the uncertainty and competing accounts in the reporting.

content.headline: COP31 ends without agreement on its central climate deal
content.shortHeadline: COP31 ends without a central climate deal
content.standfirst: Negotiators failed to agree on the summit’s main political text after more than 44 hours of overtime. The dispute centred on fossil fuels and climate finance, although other decisions from the talks will proceed.

image.caption: COP31 chair Murat Kurum announces that negotiators have no consensus on the text.

sources.originalTitle: Cop31 climate talks break down as key deal rejected
Klimatopmødet COP31 ender uden aftale

segments.body: The COP31 presidencies said there was no consensus on the proposed Antalya pact, so the summit’s central “cover decision” was not adopted. The draft called for electrification and adaptation finance but did not explicitly endorse a transition away from fossil fuels, a demand made by more than 130 countries.

segments.title: A deal divided
segments.body: The EU, UK and several developing countries rejected the text, while Pakistan and Ghana argued that its other provisions should not be discarded. The Guardian reports objections to proposed carbon-capture provisions; DR says Danish climate minister Samira Nawa described the breakdown as a chance to restart global climate diplomacy.

perspectives.body: Nawa said Denmark would not accept oil-producing countries dictating global climate policy, but framed the breakdown as a possible reset for climate diplomacy.

content.headline: Explosion hits Russian ship at Libyan port; cause and casualties disputed
content.shortHeadline: Explosion hits Russian ship in Libya; casualty reports differ
content.standfirst: An explosion and fire struck a Russian vessel at Benghazi, and satellite imagery reviewed by the BBC showed it later partly submerged. Libya’s eastern authorities said there were no casualties, while DR, citing Reuters, reported two people injured.

image.caption: Satellite imagery shows a vessel on fire at Benghazi port early on Sunday.

sources.originalTitle: Explosion on Russian ship at Libya port caused by suspected drone attack, officials say
Russisk skib ramt i formodet droneangreb i Libyen

segments.body: Libya’s eastern government said the ship was docked at Benghazi naval port for fuel and supplies on its way back to Russia when an explosion occurred around dawn on Sunday. The BBC verified satellite imagery showing a vessel on fire and later apparently partly submerged. The eastern authorities said there were no casualties; DR, citing Reuters, reported two people injured.

segments.title: Responsibility remains unknown
segments.body: The eastern government called the incident a suspected drone attack and said it was working with Russia to investigate. Moscow had not commented, and no one had claimed responsibility in the reports. Libya’s internationally recognised government in Tripoli separately warned against foreign forces using civilian facilities in external conflicts.

content.headline: Israeli settler attacks on West Bank villages draw ‘terrorism’ rebuke
content.shortHeadline: West Bank settler attacks prompt Israeli ‘terrorism’ rebuke
content.standfirst: Dozens of settlers reportedly set fire to homes and vehicles in at least four Palestinian communities. Israeli opposition figures condemned the attacks, while police said they had opened an investigation.

image.caption: Cars burned in the West Bank village of Kafr Malik after settler attacks.

sources.originalTitle: Netanyahu rival condemns ‘Jewish terrorism’ after settler attacks on Palestinian villages

segments.body: Dozens of Israeli settlers raided Palestinian communities in the occupied West Bank on Saturday night, setting fire to about a dozen vehicles and several homes, and leaving racist graffiti, according to the Guardian. Israeli police said they were investigating with forensic teams.

segments.title: Political condemnation
segments.body: Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot called the attacks “Jewish terrorism” and said they threatened regional stability and Israel’s security. Other lawmakers blamed the government’s handling of settler violence. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had not responded to the accusations in the report.

content.headline: Indonesia factory fire leaves dozens missing as rescuers recover bodies
content.shortHeadline: Dozens missing after deadly Indonesian factory fire
content.standfirst: Rescuers searching a confectionery factory in western Java said they had recovered 24 body bags, while around 36 people remained missing. The cause of the fire has not been established.

image.caption: Drone footage shows the aftermath of the factory fire in western Java.

sources.originalTitle: Three killed and dozens missing after fire at Indonesian factory

segments.body: A fire engulfed a confectionery factory in Serang district, Banten province, on Saturday. Indonesia’s search and rescue agency said 15 survivors had been located and 24 body bags recovered by Sunday evening; around 36 people were still missing. Authorities have not determined what caused the fire.

About 60 people were believed to have been inside, the Banten governor said. Rescuers were searching the damaged building, with relatives gathered outside waiting for news. Local media said the search had paused for the night and was due to resume on Monday.

content.headline: Russia-bound cargo ship still burning after Gulf of Finland drone strike
content.shortHeadline: Russian cargo ship still burning after Gulf of Finland strike
content.standfirst: Firefighting and salvage work continued on Sunday after the Sparta II was hit and drifted into Finnish waters. The crew has been evacuated; Ukraine has not commented on Finland’s assessment that it was likely behind the attack.

image.caption: Finnish authorities continue work on the damaged Sparta II.

sources.originalTitle: Russia-bound ship still on fire after attack in Gulf of Finland
What to know as Russian cargo ship ‘attacked by drones’ in the Baltic Sea

segments.body: The Sparta II, bound for Kaliningrad, was hit by a drone on Saturday and drifted into Finnish waters. Finland’s Border Guard said work was continuing to prevent it from sinking, with Estonian and Russian assets also involved. The crew had been evacuated to another Russian vessel, and authorities reported no danger to nearby traffic or environmental damage.

segments.title: An unresolved strike
segments.body: Finnish defence officials said Ukraine was likely behind the attack; Kyiv had not commented. The ship is under US and Ukrainian sanctions and is linked to a company that provides logistics services to Russia’s defence ministry. Finland said a Russian helicopter was suspected of violating its airspace, possibly during rescue or monitoring operations.

content.headline: US Army plans to detonate explosives despite court order to halt it
content.shortHeadline: US Army plans explosives detonation despite court halt
content.standfirst: The Army says five tonnes of degraded explosives at an Iowa ammunition plant risk an accidental blast as temperatures fall. Environmental groups argue that residents had little warning and have challenged the planned detonation.

sources.originalTitle: US Army to detonate tonnes of unstable explosives in Iowa despite court order

segments.body: The US Army plans to detonate five tonnes of degraded explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant by 24 November, despite a federal court order suspending the operation. The Army says the material could explode accidentally as temperatures drop and argues that destroying it in place is the safest option.

segments.title: Residents and environmental concerns
segments.body: Environmental groups sued to stop the detonation, saying the Army had not adequately considered safer alternatives. The Iowa Environmental Council also said people in the risk zone had only days to prepare for the original date and warned that lead exposure has no safe level. The Army has not disclosed a new detonation schedule.

content.headline: Fewer young Nigerians register to vote as election approaches
content.shortHeadline: Young Nigerians register to vote in lower numbers
content.standfirst: Young people now make up 29% of registered Nigerian voters, down from 40% in 2023, despite the country’s youthful population. Interviewees point to disillusionment, the cost of politics and barriers to entering established parties.

image.caption: Nigerian President Bola Tinubu is among the older candidates in the coming election.

sources.originalTitle: Nigerian youth have shown their power in the past - why aren't they shaping this election?

segments.body: Nigeria’s electoral register has grown by about 10 million since the last election, to more than 103 million, but registration among under-35s has fallen by around seven million. Young people now account for 29% of registered voters, compared with 40% in 2023, ahead of the 2027 general election.

segments.title: Barriers to participation
segments.body: Some young Nigerians told the BBC they had lost faith after earlier political movements failed to deliver change. Aspiring politicians and analysts also pointed to the expense of campaigning, steep party nomination fees and the dominance of established political networks as obstacles to younger candidates.

content.headline: Europe faces an election cycle that could test the EU’s cohesion
content.shortHeadline: Europe’s coming elections could test EU cohesion
content.standfirst: Elections in several major EU countries over the next year could strengthen nationalist and Eurosceptic parties, according to Guardian analysis. Their leaders may not be able to rewrite EU law, but could obstruct joint decisions.

image.caption: Illustration accompanying an analysis of Europe’s coming elections and the future of the EU.

sources.originalTitle: Europe is entering a ‘supercycle’ of national elections. Their outcomes could shake the EU’s foundations

segments.body: The Guardian describes an unusually concentrated election cycle, with voters in four of the EU’s five largest member states due to go to the polls by the end of 2027. It argues that nationalist and Eurosceptic parties could gain ground even as public support for EU membership remains high.

segments.title: Risks to joint action
segments.body: The analysis says a larger bloc of Eurosceptic leaders could make decisions on the EU budget, Ukraine aid, enlargement and cooperation on defence or energy harder to reach. It identifies France as a particularly consequential contest, while noting that outcomes and their effects remain uncertain.

content.headline: May tells Burnham to ‘move on’ from Brexit as closer EU ties debated
content.shortHeadline: May tells Burnham to ‘move on’ from Brexit
content.standfirst: Theresa May warned that negotiations on rejoining the EU could consume government time, while Ed Miliband argued closer integration would give Britain more say over rules it already follows. The shape and extent of future ties remain unsettled.

image.caption: Theresa May says Andy Burnham should accept Brexit and move on.

sources.originalTitle: Theresa May ‘aghast’ at Andy Burnham’s talk about rejoining EU
How a new deal on small boat migrants could be Burnham’s next Brexit prize
Burnham ready to cut tuition fees for EU students to avoid Brexit deal collapse
New Brexit deal to allow 100,000 under-32s to move to UK could be expanded
Closer EU ties will give UK say on Brussels decisions, says Ed Miliband
Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place
UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
The secret dinner where Labour grandees met to plot Brexit reversal

segments.body: After the UK and EU agreed deals on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he would brainstorm future options with the bloc. Theresa May, who led the UK’s Brexit negotiations, urged him to accept the referendum result and said talks on rejoining would absorb time across government.

segments.title: Arguments over the next step
segments.body: Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said closer ties could give the UK input into EU rules affecting British businesses, while stopping short of saying whether he backed discussions on rejoining. The Guardian reports division over how far to go; the agreements’ implementation is also linked to resolving a dispute over tuition fees for EU students.

perspectives.body: Food exporters welcomed the prospect of fewer checks, but some said they would wait for the deal to take effect in 2028 before committing to renewed trade.

content.headline: UK taxpayers’ offshore holdings exceed £1tn, HMRC figures show
content.shortHeadline: UK taxpayers’ offshore holdings top £1tn
content.standfirst: HMRC data obtained by TaxWatch shows a 10% rise in reported balances between 2022 and 2024. The figures do not establish how much is undeclared, but the thinktank says gaps in account data make some taxpayers difficult to trace.

image.caption: Road Town in the British Virgin Islands, one of the offshore financial centres included in the reporting.

sources.originalTitle: UK taxpayer funds held in offshore tax havens top £1tn, latest HMRC data shows

segments.body: Balances held offshore by UK taxpayers in jurisdictions classified as tax havens exceeded £1tn, according to the latest available HMRC data, covering 2022 to 2024. Much of the money may have been declared, but HMRC recovered an average of £125m a year in unpaid tax, interest and penalties from offshore accounts.

segments.title: Difficult to trace
segments.body: TaxWatch says roughly a fifth of UK-owned offshore accounts reported through an international information-sharing system lacked a unique taxpayer identifier, making it harder to match accounts to individuals. HMRC says it is adding 400 people to tackle wealthy offshore non-compliance by 2030.

content.headline: Inquiry finds failures before Exeter man killed three during psychotic episode
content.shortHeadline: Exeter killer was released after a ‘catalogue of failures’
content.standfirst: A joint investigation found that police and medical staff missed warnings and released Alexander Lewis-Ranwell twice in the 48 hours before he killed three men in 2019. Their families say they are still waiting for answers and an apology.

image.caption: Alexander Lewis-Ranwell is released from a police station.

sources.originalTitle: Man who killed three during psychotic episode ‘had been released after catalogue of failures’

segments.body: Alexander Lewis-Ranwell, who had paranoid schizophrenia, was arrested twice and released in the 48 hours before killing Anthony Payne and twins Roger and Dick Carter in Exeter in 2019. A joint investigation by the Sunday Times and BBC Radio 4 found that warnings about his mental health and behaviour were missed or not shared.

segments.title: Families still seek answers
segments.body: An inquest last month found failings by police had contributed to Lewis-Ranwell’s release. His victims’ families want the police watchdog to investigate the force; the watchdog said it had not received a request for a review. Devon and Cornwall Police said it was addressing areas of learning.

content.headline: Proposed UK residency changes leave long-term migrants uncertain
content.shortHeadline: Migrants say residency changes leave them in limbo
content.standfirst: People who expected to qualify for permanent residency under the 10-year long-residence route say proposed changes could reset their progress. The government says settlement should be earned through contribution and compliance.

image.caption: Harry Mithun says he planned his life around qualifying for permanent residency after nine years in the UK.

sources.originalTitle: Indefinite leave to remain changes are a betrayal – I’ve been here for nine years

segments.body: The UK plans to scrap the 10-year Long Residence route to indefinite leave to remain, but has not yet announced when the change will take effect. The new framework also proposes extending the standard qualifying period from five to 10 years, with shorter routes for some higher earners.

segments.title: People facing a reset
segments.body: Several migrants told the i Paper that years spent in the UK on student or graduate visas may no longer count towards settlement. One man who moved from Sri Lanka in 2017 said the change could add at least a decade to his wait; the Home Office said those who contribute most will settle fastest.

content.headline: Experts warn of rise in far-right vigilantes posing as security
content.shortHeadline: Experts warn of far-right ‘security’ vigilantes
content.standfirst: A volunteer group seen at far-right protests and alongside prominent figures says its members do not need security licences. A security-industry representative says the uniforms could mislead or intimidate the public.

image.caption: Members of British Security UK at a youth strike in Parliament Square.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Intimidating’ vigilantes posing as far-right security on the rise, UK experts say

segments.body: Members of British Security UK, a volunteer group whose members wear black uniforms and body armour, have appeared at far-right protests and alongside figures including Tommy Robinson and Britain First leader Paul Golding. The Guardian reports that volunteers are not required to have security qualifications or training.

segments.title: Dispute over licensing
segments.body: A security-industry representative called the group vigilantes and said the clothing could lead the public to mistake members for legitimate security staff. Its director argues that genuinely unpaid volunteers do not require a licence. The Home Office said anyone who breaks the law will face the full force of the law.

content.headline: NHS hospitals prepare to offer Alzheimer’s blood tests sooner
content.shortHeadline: Alzheimer’s blood tests set to reach more NHS hospitals
content.standfirst: Some hospitals plan to offer tests from early 2027 that could shorten diagnosis from months or years to days. Trials are ongoing, access may vary between areas and doctors warn against using private tests without a clinical assessment.

image.caption: A blood sample could help doctors assess whether memory problems are caused by Alzheimer’s.

sources.originalTitle: Blood tests that cut Alzheimer’s diagnosis from years to days coming in early 2027

segments.body: Blood tests measuring a form of tau protein could help identify Alzheimer’s disease and distinguish it from other causes of memory problems. University College Hospital in London already offers the test, and Manchester Brain Health Centre says it plans to begin within weeks; more hospitals are considering it.

segments.title: Access and caution
segments.body: Two large trials are assessing how the tests fit into NHS care and are due to finish in 2029. There is no central list of hospitals offering them, raising the prospect of uneven access. Doctors also caution that private testing outside a memory clinic could produce false positives.

content.headline: Tønder mayor charged over alleged mistreatment of more than 150 pigs
content.shortHeadline: Tønder mayor charged over alleged pig mistreatment
content.standfirst: A TV 2 review of the indictment describes repeated animal-welfare violations found during five inspections of Jørgen Popp Petersen’s farm. He has said he was surprised to be charged; the allegations have not been proved in court.

image.caption: Tønder mayor Jørgen Popp Petersen, who has been charged in an animal-welfare case.

source.credit: Foto: Mikkel Berg Pedersen / Ritzau Scanpix

sources.originalTitle: Dyrlæge overrasket over detaljer i anklageskrift mod borgmester

segments.body: The indictment accuses Tønder mayor Jørgen Popp Petersen of animal-welfare offences at his farm, including cases involving more than 150 pigs. A veterinarian who reviewed the document for TV 2 said the alleged conditions were among the more serious she had seen.

segments.title: Repeated inspection findings
segments.body: The indictment covers five inspections between October 2022 and November 2024, with allegations including sick or injured pigs, inadequate care and repeated problems after earlier inspections. Petersen declined a TV 2 interview and told TV Syd he was surprised to be charged. Prosecutors are seeking prison sentences.

content.headline: New inspections find pests and mould at Danish Agro grain warehouses
content.shortHeadline: Danish Agro warehouses face fresh pest criticism
content.standfirst: Autumn inspections found rodents, mould and other signs of pests at two sites, prompting the company to close them as food-storage facilities. Danish Agro says it is upgrading buildings and reviewing pest control.

image.caption: A Danish Agro representative faces questions about warehouse conditions after fresh inspection findings.

sources.originalTitle: Rotteproblemer hos Danish Agro fortsætter i år – flere haller må lukke

segments.body: Food inspectors found rodent droppings, dead and live rodents and signs of mould at Danish Agro warehouses in Lille Skensved and Kirke Stillinge this autumn, according to TV 2 and Politiken. At the latter site, an inspector reported that a rat jumped onto their leg during a visit.

segments.title: Company response and unresolved questions
segments.body: Danish Agro said the Kirke Stillinge site failed to meet its own or the authorities’ standards and that both sites were closed for food storage. It says it is upgrading buildings and testing grain to determine whether it can be used for food, animal feed or biogas. TV 2 says the company did not specify how some grain stored outdoors had been used.

content.headline: European forces train for a possible postwar security mission in Ukraine
content.shortHeadline: European forces rehearse a possible Ukraine security mission
content.standfirst: Around 2,800 troops from 11 countries took part in the first exercise for a proposed European-led force to support Ukraine after a possible peace deal. Denmark, despite backing the coalition, sent no soldiers to the exercise.

image.caption: A Polish air-defence unit takes part in the exercise for a proposed European force supporting Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: Europæiske soldater træner vigtig Ukraine-mission, men danskerne blev hjemme

segments.body: Troops from 11 countries trained in eastern Poland for a possible European security mission in Ukraine after a peace agreement. The two-week exercise involved around 2,800 personnel and was led by France and the UK. Denmark contributed at staff level but did not send soldiers.

segments.title: A plan with unanswered questions
segments.body: The proposed force is described as a reassurance and security presence, not a combat force. Its mandate, the contributions individual countries would make and how it would operate in the face of Russian opposition remain uncertain. Denmark’s vice-defence chief said any future contribution could involve troops, aircraft or naval forces.

content.headline: Mathematician says AI helped produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis
content.shortHeadline: AI-assisted proof of Riemann hypothesis awaits scrutiny
content.standfirst: An Anthropic mathematician says he used the company’s Claude model to develop a detailed proof of a problem that has resisted mathematicians for 167 years. Experts have yet to establish that people understand the proof or that it is correct.

image.caption: Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei at the company’s stock-market listing.

sources.originalTitle: I 167 år har ingen løst det. Nu har matematiker knækket koden med AI

segments.body: Levent Alpöge says he developed a proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis in six weeks while working with Anthropic’s Claude model. The hypothesis, dating to 1859, concerns the distribution of prime numbers and is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute’s Millennium problems.

segments.title: Verification still ahead
segments.body: The proof is written in the Lean computer language and runs to more than 250,000 pages, according to DR. A University of Copenhagen mathematician said the formal system can check the result, but no person yet understands why it is correct. The claim remains subject to scrutiny.

content.headline: Small Danish shops warn fuel-tax cut could leave them selling at a loss
content.shortHeadline: Small shops fear losses after proposed fuel-tax cut
content.standfirst: Several local shops say they could lose money on fuel already bought at higher prices if parliament cuts petrol and diesel duties next week. The potential losses are uncertain, and the businesses are asking for support.

sources.originalTitle: Købmænd i nødråb om benzinafgift

segments.body: Independent shops in Gudumholm, Øster Assels and Øster Hornum say a proposed two-kroner-per-litre cut to petrol and diesel duties could leave them selling existing stock below what they paid. The cut is expected to take effect on 1 December if parliament approves it.

Gudumholm’s shop has urged customers to fill up while prices are still high, hoping to reduce its exposure. DR reports that a similar shop in Øster Assels could lose as much as 60,000 kroner, though the loss at Gudumholm has not been calculated. The shop says it would like compensation.

content.headline: Danish researcher says attitudes to divorce are changing in some minority groups
content.shortHeadline: Changing attitudes to divorce among some Danish minorities
content.standfirst: A Danish woman who celebrated her divorce says family support helped her manage stigma and other people’s expectations. A researcher sees signs of changing attitudes among people with Muslim backgrounds, while stressing that experiences vary.

image.caption: A cake marked “finally divorced” was served at Dania Kader’s celebration.

sources.originalTitle: Hun blev skilt – så inviterede hun til fest

segments.body: Dania Kader celebrated her divorce with family after ending her marriage when her daughter was about eight months old. She said support from her parents helped her through the decision and made it easier to withstand gossip and pressure to give the marriage another chance.

segments.title: Change across generations
segments.body: VIVE professor Anika Liversage said divorce is becoming more common among Danes with Muslim backgrounds, which may make it easier for others to choose the same path. She stressed that attitudes differ between communities and that some groups may continue to make divorce difficult.

content.headline: Danish Home Guard aircraft begins two-month Frontex mission in Spain
content.shortHeadline: Danish aircraft begins two-month Frontex mission
content.standfirst: A volunteer crew and Twin Otter aircraft are heading to Málaga to support EU border patrols in the Mediterranean. The mission will focus on maritime monitoring, including drug and weapons smuggling and migrant routes.

image.caption: A Danish Home Guard Twin Otter heads to Málaga for the Frontex mission.

sources.originalTitle: Hjemmeværnsfly har kurs mod Spanien for at beskytte EU's grænser

segments.body: A Danish Home Guard Twin Otter aircraft and volunteer personnel are beginning a two-month mission supporting Frontex from Málaga. Their maritime surveillance will focus on issues including drug and weapons smuggling and migration routes around the Mediterranean.

content.headline: Stella Z turns field recordings and lucid dreams into ambient soundscapes
content.shortHeadline: Stella Z’s ambient dreams draw on recordings from China
content.standfirst: The Fujian-born, London-based producer builds a nocturnal collage from sounds gathered on trips to China. Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming drifts between ambient, dub and acid, with unease sometimes lending its most vivid moments their charge.

image.caption: Stella Z, the Fujian-born, London-based producer.

sources.originalTitle: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming

segments.body: Sounds recorded on Stella Z’s trips to China—among them a pharmacy and the Fujian mountains at night—give Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming its unusual sense of place. Across eight tracks, whispers, percussion and electronics create an unsettled, dreamlike collage.

The album moves through ambient and new-age expanses, with traces of 1990s downtempo, acid and dub. “Exit, Elsewhere” grows disorientating through overlapping narration and rattling bells; a remix by Valentina Magaletti turns the original’s wistfulness into something harsher. Even its clumsier passages help conjure a woozy wilderness.

content.headline: Kate Nash turns music-industry frustration into a fight for touring artists
content.shortHeadline: Kate Nash challenges a music business that makes touring precarious
content.standfirst: The singer’s OnlyFans-funded “Butts for Tour Buses” campaign made the cost of touring hard to ignore. Her forthcoming album Cailín draws on Irish roots, while she argues that fair pay for working musicians requires more than goodwill.

image.caption: Kate Nash.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I have to sell my bum on OnlyFans to go on tour’: Kate Nash on fame, feminism and fighting the music business

segments.body: In 2024, Kate Nash used an OnlyFans account to help fund a tour and staged a protest outside Spotify and Live Nation. She says even artists with established catalogues struggle to make touring work, while friends sell instruments or abandon the road altogether. Without small and mid-sized gigs, she argues, the wider music culture is at risk.

segments.title: A record rooted in family history
segments.body: On Cailín, recorded in Spiddal on Ireland’s west coast, Nash combines traditional instruments with punk and hip-hop as she explores her Irish heritage. The album includes a cover of Sinéad O’Connor’s “Famine”, and follows Nash’s discovery that her grandfather was among men imprisoned while trying to travel to Spain to fight Franco.

segments.title: Making a case for change
segments.body: Nash says the music industry will not reform itself and argues that legislation is needed to make payment fairer. Her account traces the distance between early fame and a career she has rebuilt on her own terms, including acting work and an independent approach to making music.

content.headline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul turn grief into playful, personal pop
content.shortHeadline: Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul get personal on a new album
content.standfirst: The Belgian duo’s second album, Mainland Madinina, follows a period of grief and becoming parents. Their familiar wit remains, but the new songs also make room for vulnerability, family history and questions about what gets passed on.

image.caption: Bolis Pupul and Charlotte Adigéry.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Would you breastfeed your own father?’ The goofy, spiky world of art-pop duo Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul

segments.body: After the sharp, politically minded pop of their debut, Charlotte Adigéry and Bolis Pupul describe their forthcoming album as more introspective. They began writing it after Adigéry’s father died, and worked on early demos during a trip to Martinique, her parents’ birthplace.

segments.title: Humour alongside grief
segments.body: The record still makes room for absurdity: “Googoo Gaga” plays with parenthood, while “From Healer to Dealer” sends up wellness language. But closing song “I’m Lost” turns toward Adigéry’s grief, as she sings about finally throwing away flowers from her father’s funeral. The album also considers how becoming a parent can bring family trauma into focus.

segments.title: Pop as a Trojan horse
segments.body: The duo say they first recognised the political reach of their music when a Manchester crowd sang along to the deliberately provocative chorus of “Blenda”. Their aim, they explain, is to trust listeners to understand the joke and the ideas carried inside the pop.

content.headline: Radie Peat’s debut solo album makes centuries of folk feel immediate
content.shortHeadline: Radie Peat brings centuries of folk into the present
content.standfirst: The Lankum singer gathers songs from Irish, British and American traditions, centring complex women’s stories. Her commanding voice anchors arrangements that move from stark folk to a striking trip-hop reworking.

sources.originalTitle: No Human Tongue Can Tell

segments.body: Radie Peat opens No Human Tongue Can Tell with the traditional “Hares on the Mountain”, her voice coming in before the piano. The Lankum and ØXN singer plays nearly every instrument on this solo debut, building layered choruses around a voice the review describes as an arresting contralto.

segments.title: Songs that speak across time
segments.body: Peat draws on Irish, British and American songbooks, with particular attention to women whose choices are constrained. The tracklist sets older songs alongside more recent compositions, finding connections between a story of abuse and Liam Weldon’s lament for the frustrated promise of Irish independence.

The boldest transformation is “The Moon and Stars”, which turns the archived fiddle tune “Maid Lamenting” into a trip-hop piece with a skittering beat and surging keyboards. Peat’s performance cuts through the dense production, drawing the album’s distant musical eras into a vivid present.

content.headline: Thoom fuses hyperpop and Arabic instrumentation into a volatile debut
content.shortHeadline: Thoom makes hyperpop collide with Arabic instrumentation
content.standfirst: On Everyday, Everything Is at Stake, Beirut-born, Los Angeles-based artist Zeynab Marwan puts her voice at the centre of a dramatic mix of hyperpop production and Arabic instruments. The result connects club aggression to longing and belonging.

sources.originalTitle: Everyday, Everything Is at Stake

segments.body: As Thoom, Zeynab Marwan joins producers Dylan Brady and Ike Clateman on a debut that brings hyperpop into contact with Arabic instrumentation. Her voice shifts from syrupy melody to a more menacing edge, and the review hears an artist moving beyond the more atmospheric approach of her earlier releases.

segments.title: Fury and feeling
segments.body: Tracks such as “Janani” and “On the Floor” build around forceful drums and mizmar, while “Morocco” uses oud and slower machines to frame a lover’s hurt. The review praises the way the production amplifies Marwan’s performances, though it finds some of the more conventional songs less distinctive.

The closing song, “I’m Going Back to Lebanon”, holds together a farewell to a lover and a desire to return to Marwan’s homeland. Its unanswered questions about return and renewed conflict give the album’s themes of attachment and uncertainty their clearest expression.

content.headline: R.E.M.’s Reveal reissue shows how a once-overlooked album shaped indie-pop
content.shortHeadline: R.E.M.’s Reveal reissue points toward indie-pop’s future
content.standfirst: The band’s 2001 move toward warm synth-pop, once overshadowed by its earlier work, sounds newly influential on a 25th-anniversary edition. The review also finds fresh life in a set of archival live performances.

sources.originalTitle: Reveal (25th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: Recorded after drummer Bill Berry’s retirement, Reveal shifted R.E.M. toward a more reflective sound, with strings and electronics replacing some of the band’s earlier rock mysticism. The review argues the album’s dreamy, synth-pop arrangements now look like a precursor to later indie-pop.

segments.title: A reissue with room to roam
segments.body: The review singles out “All the Way to Reno (You’re Gonna Be a Star)” and “Imitation of Life”, while bonus material captures the expanded band playing for Radio France. Familiar songs take on different textures in performance, from organ in “So. Central Rain” to piano and massed vocals on “It’s the End of the World as We Know It (and I Feel Fine)”.

content.headline: Kim Deal’s Barbican concert album lets her personality shine through
content.shortHeadline: Kim Deal’s live album adds orchestral warmth to her songs
content.standfirst: A 13-piece orchestra and choir expand the arrangements from Kim Deal’s solo debut on this London concert recording. It is less a radical reinvention than an affectionate showcase for her distinctive voice.

sources.originalTitle: Live at the Barbican

segments.body: Recorded at London’s Barbican, the concert album draws mostly on Kim Deal’s solo debut, with a few earlier solo songs and Breeders material. The orchestral arrangements largely stay faithful to the studio versions, but the review finds that their strings and brass add subtle warmth and scale.

The orchestra makes a particular difference on “Beautiful Moon”, where cello gives the spare original a more haunting shape. The Shards choir is less prominent, but Deal herself takes centre stage: her rough-edged, expressive delivery brings vulnerability and force to “Walking With a Killer”.

content.headline: Threshold’s new folk-prog sound leads a week of adventurous tracks
content.shortHeadline: Threshold leads a week of adventurous new tracks
content.standfirst: Isaac Eiger’s solo project moves beyond the jangle-pop of Strange Ranger toward folk and loose, minimalist prog. The Guardian’s weekly picks also span experimental pop, UK rap, jazz and more.

image.caption: Threshold, Isaac Eiger’s solo project.

sources.originalTitle: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold

segments.body: Threshold’s “Stillwater” stretches out like a wintry walk, drawing on 1970s singer-songwriter piano ballads while pointing toward the wider sound of Isaac Eiger’s forthcoming debut album. The former Strange Ranger frontman’s new material reaches into traditional folk and minimalist prog, leaving his earlier jangle-pop behind.

segments.title: More to hear this week
segments.body: The roundup’s other picks include Heavensouls’ ten-minute experimental piece, a noirish collaboration from BexBlu and Paul Stephan, new tracks from Erika de Casier and Rema, and music by Studio20, Kacey Musgraves and Brazilian duo João Bosco and Guto Wirtti.

content.headline: Paul Schrader embraces AI for filmmaking, even as he fears what it may unleash
content.shortHeadline: Paul Schrader is using AI—and worries it could outgrow him
content.standfirst: The Taxi Driver writer is testing AI-generated actors, scripts and hallucinations for new projects. He sees the technology as hard to resist, but says asking it to write in his own style left him frightened by its capabilities.

image.caption: Paul Schrader, who is experimenting with AI in filmmaking.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I’m opening the cage of a monster’: Taxi Driver scriptwriter Paul Schrader on unleashing AI at 80

segments.body: At 80, Paul Schrader is using artificial intelligence to develop films, including horror-thriller The Doors of Perception, which will feature AI-generated psychedelic visions. He has also tested synthetic actors and says the technology could make a whole film, while giving him an unusually easy route around the costs and delays of conventional production.

segments.title: A tool that unsettled its user
segments.body: Schrader says an AI system proposed premises for a script in his style, then produced a scene-by-scene outline and a formatted opening scene. The speed and resemblance to his own writing startled him. “I realised it could write a Paul Schrader script. I got scared,” he said.

segments.title: Hollywood’s unresolved argument
segments.body: While unions and institutions have tried to set limits on AI in film, Schrader believes financial incentives will make it difficult to stop. He also voices a much broader fear that humans may have no lasting place in a world shaped by increasingly capable machines; what remains unclear is how audiences will respond to films made this way.

content.headline: Wicker’s knowingly sexist fairy tale turns a perfect husband into a provocation
content.shortHeadline: Wicker’s impossible husband makes for a provocative comedy
content.standfirst: Olivia Colman plays a fisherwoman who commissions a husband made of twigs in this bawdy medieval fantasy. Its reviewer enjoys the comedy but questions the story’s vision of a partner whose own desires barely count.

image.caption: Olivia Colman as the fisherwoman who commissions a husband made of wicker.

sources.originalTitle: Wicker is unhinged and sexist. I loved it

segments.body: In Wicker, a lonely fisherwoman played by Olivia Colman pays a basketmaker to create her a husband. Alexander Skarsgård’s woven creation is attentive, attractive and seemingly devoted to pleasing her, setting off lust, envy and alarm in the village around them.

segments.title: Fantasy with a sharp edge
segments.body: The review relishes the film’s bawdy humour and argues that its fantasy of a considerate partner responds to familiar inequalities in heterosexual relationships. But it also sees a troubling premise: the husband’s agency is barely explored, and his wife’s wishes take priority even when he objects.

The reviewer finds the film’s contradictions hard to dismiss—and ultimately enjoys it. Colman’s fisherwoman seems to want kindness rather than obedience, but the story’s deliberately excessive reversal raises a question it does not quite resolve: when devotion is built into a partner, can it be freely given?

content.headline: Josephine asks what happens after a child witnesses sexual violence
content.shortHeadline: Josephine explores a child’s trauma after witnessing rape
content.standfirst: Director Beth de Araújo draws on her own experience for a drama about an eight-year-old who witnesses a rape. The film’s approach has prompted debate over how cinema should depict sexual violence and protect young performers.

sources.originalTitle: 'The subject is still taboo': Shocking new film Josephine confronts sexual violence through a child's eyes

segments.body: In Josephine, an eight-year-old girl witnesses a rape in a park, an event that shapes the story of her and her parents, played by Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan. Writer-director Beth de Araújo says the film draws on her own childhood experience and asks how a young person might understand violence before having words for it.

segments.title: Questions about showing violence
segments.body: The film depicts the assault from a distance through the child’s perspective. Film scholar Tanya Horeck says there is no single feminist rule for representing rape on screen, but asks what a scene is doing and whose perspective it serves. She finds the case for placing the scene early in Josephine compelling because the film follows the child’s trauma.

segments.title: Protecting a young actor
segments.body: Reeves, who was eight during filming, did not read the script or appear during the assault scene, and has not seen the finished film. De Araújo says a child psychologist was available to the family and that Reeves can choose whether to watch the film when she is 18.

content.headline: Oobah Butler’s pranks expose how easily industries can be gamed
content.shortHeadline: Oobah Butler turns industry loopholes into comedy
content.standfirst: In a new series, the prankster infiltrates sectors from wellness to music, testing their appetite for bogus products and manufactured hype. The review finds the stunts funny—and an unsettling look at gullibility and weak regulation.

image.caption: Oobah Butler in Scams for a Better Tomorrow.

sources.originalTitle: Oobah Butler: Scams for a Better Tomorrow review – these audacious pranks are tell-your-friends funny

segments.body: Oobah Butler’s five-part series takes his stunts inside industries including wellness, wine, dating, music and royalty. He sells fake wellness products, markets smoke-damaged wine at a premium and tries to make a machine-written song trend, presenting the schemes as experiments as well as jokes.

segments.title: The joke has a target
segments.body: The review praises Butler’s boldness and argues that his pranks mostly take aim at institutions rather than individuals. A former Theranos executive even appears to advise him on marketing, a pointed detail in a show about how readily dubious claims can be sold.

Behind the comic set-ups, the series finds loopholes, weak regulation and investors willing to back far-fetched schemes. The review’s broader verdict is that Butler’s pranks are both disquieting and unexpectedly reassuring: they expose how easily systems can be exploited, while making their targets laughable.

content.headline: The BBC is putting some Christmas specials on iPlayer weeks early
content.shortHeadline: The BBC is moving some Christmas TV specials earlier
content.standfirst: Several festive programmes will arrive on iPlayer from 27 November, ahead of their television broadcasts. The BBC says a longer streaming window reflects viewing habits, while the change leaves questions about the shared ritual of Christmas TV.

image.caption: Mary Berry filming her Christmas Countdown.

sources.originalTitle: ‘In the office, there was a sharp intake of breath’: why has the BBC decided to celebrate Christmas earlier than ever?

segments.body: The BBC plans to make several Christmas specials available on iPlayer from 27 November, in some cases almost a month before they air on television. The broadcaster says viewing of festive programmes has grown earlier in the season and that the longer window may help programmes find an audience.

segments.title: A change to a shared schedule
segments.body: Some major Christmas broadcasts, including the Strictly special and the new Call the Midwife prequel, remain scheduled for television as usual. Radio Times editor Shem Law says the earlier streaming releases may nevertheless weaken the appeal of gathering around a programme together when it finally airs.

content.headline: Melania’s two-part TV documentary offers little beyond its subject’s image
content.shortHeadline: Melania’s TV documentary is more advert than series
content.standfirst: A review finds the two short episodes almost empty of substance, apart from a brief encounter with people affected by natural disasters. The programme repeatedly turns its attention back to Melania Trump and her projects.

image.caption: Melania Trump.

sources.originalTitle: Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space

segments.body: The review describes Melania as two episodes of short, disconnected scenes rather than a substantial series. It criticises the programme’s polished footage and vague statements, including an extended sequence in which Melania Trump considers the placement of a brooch.

A visit with people affected by Hurricane Helene and wildfires briefly shifts the programme toward their experiences. But the review says it soon returns to Trump’s own initiatives, leaving little room for the people the series appears to be documenting.

content.headline: I Am Helen puts the consequences of toxic masculinity in the foreground
content.shortHeadline: I Am Helen shows the cost of toxic masculinity for women
content.standfirst: Nicola Coughlan plays a woman whose partner’s coercive behaviour escalates in the latest instalment of Dominic Savage’s drama anthology. The review argues that the series centres the women who are often overlooked in stories about male violence.

image.caption: Nicola Coughlan as Helen and Joe Cole as Steve in I Am Helen.

sources.originalTitle: All men should watch I Am Helen

segments.body: Helen, played by Nicola Coughlan, is in a seemingly ordinary relationship until her partner Steve chokes her without consent during sex. The review focuses on the aftermath: he presents himself as the victim, and Helen ends up apologising before their life returns to normal.

segments.title: The violence of the everyday
segments.body: The review argues that the drama’s disturbing force comes from how ordinary Steve’s behaviour can seem. His grievances about masculinity are reinforced by a friend and grow into coercion and anger, while Helen recognises the pattern but struggles to make him listen.

Rather than centre the destructive man, the episode makes the consequences for his partner its focus. The review sees this shift as an important contribution to television’s treatment of toxic masculinity, while stressing that men’s insecurity does not erase the harm women experience.

content.headline: Black Doves returns with Keira Knightley’s conflicted spy at its centre
content.shortHeadline: Black Doves returns to its mix of violence and feeling
content.standfirst: The cast and creator discuss the Netflix thriller’s second season, where Helen faces new risks as her husband nears Downing Street. Its murderous antiheroes, they say, work because the show keeps their humour and humanity in view.

image.caption: Keira Knightley as Helen Webb in Black Doves.

sources.originalTitle: Keira Knightley on Black Doves: ‘The violence is like a video game’

segments.body: Keira Knightley returns as Helen Webb, a spy whose marriage to a politician is bound up with her work for the Black Doves organisation. In the new season, she searches for her missing handler while facing the consequences of her husband’s rise to No 10.

segments.title: Violence with consequences
segments.body: Knightley says the show’s violence can feel like a video game before a sudden moment brings the human cost into focus. Creator Joe Barton says the series tries to acknowledge how violence is normalised in spy stories, even as it asks viewers to care about characters who have killed many people.

Ambika Mod joins as Laila Joshi, a rogue agent who becomes an uneasy ally to Helen. Knightley describes the women’s relationship as an entertaining mix of antagonism and dependence, while Barton says the new season was difficult to shape after several versions of its opening episode.

content.headline: A week’s streaming picks include a new Blade Runner series and Oobah Butler
content.shortHeadline: What to stream: Blade Runner 2099, Oobah Butler and more
content.standfirst: A new Blade Runner miniseries and Oobah Butler’s prank-driven show lead this week’s selection, alongside a Buffalo blizzard documentary, Jennifer Lopez in concert and a BBC Christmas ghost story.

image.caption: Michelle Yeoh as Olwen and Hunter Schafer as Cora in Blade Runner 2099.

sources.originalTitle: Blade Runner 2099 to Alan Carr’s Great Big Bucket List: the seven best shows to stream this week

segments.body: Blade Runner 2099 brings Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer to a new story in the franchise, while Oobah Butler’s latest series takes his elaborate hoaxes into different industries. Both are among the Guardian’s picks for new films and programmes to stream this week.

segments.title: More to watch
segments.body: The selection also includes a partly animated documentary about a community sheltering together during a deadly Buffalo blizzard, Jennifer Lopez’s Las Vegas concert film, and a BBC adaptation of a Charles Dickens ghost story. The listings provide a range of options across streaming services and broadcast television.

content.headline: GTA VI claims a record launch, with Rockstar reporting $3.79bn in first-day US$
content.shortHeadline: Rockstar says GTA VI made $3.79bn on launch day
content.standfirst: Rockstar says Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, a figure that would make the game’s launch exceptionally large across entertainment. The company’s estimate has not been independently verified in the supplied reporting.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A new record for entertainment’: Grand Theft Auto VI sales hit $3.8bn on first day of release, developer says

segments.body: Rockstar Games says Grand Theft Auto VI generated $3.79bn in retail sales on its first day, based on the company’s estimates through the end of launch day. The publisher calls it the biggest entertainment launch in history; that comparison is Rockstar’s claim.

segments.title: A record-setting release
segments.body: Rockstar says 32.5 million copies had been sold before release, and that the launch figure is nearly five times the first-day sales reported for GTA V in 2013. The game went on sale for PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S.

The same report notes that police departments urged the public not to imitate the game’s car thefts and other crimes in real life. It also says there is insufficient evidence of a scientific causal link between violent video games and violent behaviour, according to the American Psychological Association.

content.headline: Elden Ring’s film adaptation faces the challenge of making its world matter
content.shortHeadline: Can an Elden Ring film make its vast world matter?
content.standfirst: Alex Garland’s adaptation has a reported budget near $200m and a major cast, but the game’s horror-tinged fantasy world is not a story by itself. The feature weighs the challenge of giving its setting a reason to hold an audience.

image.caption: A scene from Elden Ring.

sources.originalTitle: Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation is on course to be Hollywood’s goriest ever fantasy movie

segments.body: The Guardian’s feature treats Alex Garland’s Elden Ring adaptation as an unusually high-stakes attempt to bring a vast game world to cinema. The film is reported to be in post-production, with a cast including Cailee Spaeny, Ben Whishaw and Nick Offerman; its budget is said to be close to $200m.

segments.title: A world is not a story
segments.body: The article points to earlier fantasy adaptations that struggled to turn elaborate settings into compelling films. Elden Ring’s landscape is especially grim, populated by grotesque creatures and survivors living amid death, leaving open questions about who audiences will follow and what the film’s narrative will be.

Leaked images have prompted speculation that the film may draw on events before the game, but the feature presents that as a possibility rather than a confirmed approach. Garland’s history of resisting conventional reassurance may suit the material, though the scale of the reported budget raises questions about how much freedom he will have.

content.headline: GTA VI is not for children, despite its appeal as a blockbuster game
content.shortHeadline: Why GTA VI’s 18 rating matters for parents
content.standfirst: The review praises Rockstar’s ambitious game but details its explicit sex, drugs and violence. Its central advice to parents is straightforward: the 18 rating signals adult content, not a difficulty level.

sources.originalTitle: Parents: please don’t buy Grand Theft Auto VI for your child

segments.body: The Guardian’s reviewer calls Grand Theft Auto VI an impressive and sometimes touching game, but says it is among the most explicit they have played. Its crime story includes graphic violence, full-frontal nudity, sex scenes and extensive drug use.

segments.title: A rating is a content warning
segments.body: The piece describes sexual material in the main story and in optional settings, alongside adult dialogue on the game’s fictional radio and television. The reviewer’s concern is not that adults should avoid such content, but that parents may mistake an 18 rating for a measure of difficulty rather than a warning about subject matter.

After more than 70 hours with the game, the reviewer’s advice is that it is not suitable for young children. The article suggests parents consider whether they would let their child watch Breaking Bad, while recognising that older teenagers’ experiences and maturity differ.

content.headline: Keepsake County turns suburban burglary into a melancholy stealth game
content.shortHeadline: Keepsake County makes a lonely life of theft playable
content.standfirst: This small stealth game sends a debt-ridden burglar through garish Midwestern homes, where even the loot can be a half-eaten pizza or cheap ornament. Its comic oddities sit alongside a bleak account of financial precarity.

image.caption: A scene from Keepsake County.

sources.originalTitle: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience

segments.body: In Keepsake County, Samuel breaks into suburban homes and steals what he can carry, from golf clubs to half-eaten food. He avoids killing residents, instead tying them up with improvised restraints, and takes his haul to a pawn shop rather than building a conventional arsenal of upgrades.

segments.title: Comedy with a hard edge
segments.body: The review likens the game’s eccentric art and bleak humour to a low-budget television comedy, while noting how Samuel’s medical debts and legal fees make each break-in feel less like a route to success than an act of survival. Its quiet loading-screen landscapes reinforce the character’s isolation.

The game’s repetitive robberies can feel one-note, and the review notes repeated dialogue and limited differences between regions. Yet it argues that the repetition also gives the routine its melancholy force: Samuel has little chance of escaping the conditions that keep sending him back into other people’s homes.

content.headline: Union says it has lost confidence in UK science funder over planned cuts
content.shortHeadline: Union loses confidence in UK science funder over planned cuts
content.standfirst: Prospect says UKRI’s cost-saving plans could damage national science capability and were launched without proper consultation. UKRI’s board and the science minister say they back its chief executive and reform programme.

image.caption: Jodrell Bank Observatory, whose future is at risk under planned UKRI funding changes.

sources.originalTitle: CEO of funding agency for UK science and research criticised by union over cuts

segments.body: Prospect, a union representing scientists and engineers, says it has lost confidence in Ian Chapman, chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), over planned cuts and changes to research facilities. General secretary Mike Clancy urged UKRI to pause its voluntary exit scheme and consult unions on the potential impact.

segments.title: What is at stake
segments.body:
The Science and Technology Facilities Council, part of UKRI, needs to save £162m by 2030. Plans put the future of the UK’s largest telescope at Jodrell Bank at risk, while the Clara accelerator facility is to be mothballed. Other facilities, including Diamond Light Source, are expected to make efficiency savings.

UKRI says it has engaged with staff and research communities and must keep costs within its budget. Its chair, Leszek Borysiewicz, and science minister Chris McDonald both expressed confidence in Chapman and defended the programme as a way to focus resources and deliver value for money.

content.headline: UK hospitals prepare to use Alzheimer’s blood tests before trials conclude
content.shortHeadline: Alzheimer’s blood tests set to reach more UK hospitals
content.standfirst: Some hospitals are introducing a test that may help identify Alzheimer’s within days of a memory-clinic visit, rather than after months or years. Trials are still under way, and access may vary by location.

image.caption: A blood test could help doctors assess people with memory problems for Alzheimer’s.

sources.originalTitle: Blood tests that cut Alzheimer’s diagnosis from years to days coming in early 2027

segments.body: A number of UK hospitals are preparing to offer blood tests for Alzheimer’s as part of routine care, with Manchester Brain Health Centre expecting to start within weeks. The test measures a form of tau protein, ptau217, and may help clinicians distinguish Alzheimer’s from other causes of memory problems. University College Hospital in London is already offering it.

segments.title: Earlier diagnosis, uneven access
segments.body:
A faster result could help people and their families plan and may allow some patients to access treatment or clinical trials sooner. Two large trials assessing how the tests fit into NHS services are not due to finish until 2029; hospitals can introduce them earlier, but there is no central register of providers.

That leaves a potential postcode lottery. Doctors also caution that tests bought privately outside a memory-clinic assessment could produce false positives. A blood result is part of a clinical assessment, not a standalone diagnosis.

content.headline: Climate scientists clash over a proposed delay to the IPCC’s next report
content.shortHeadline: Dispute over timing and representation delays IPCC report
content.standfirst: Some governments want the IPCC’s next assessment delayed until after a key climate stocktake, while other countries and scientists warn that a hold-up could weaken global cooperation. The dispute also centres on representation and whose assumptions shape the analysis.

sources.originalTitle: IPCC report delay will threaten global effort to tackle climate crisis, says top scientist

segments.body: The IPCC’s next assessment is under way and is hoped to be completed in 2028, in time to inform the 2028 global stocktake under the Paris agreement. Russia, India and the Arab group, including Saudi Arabia, have argued for publication in 2029 instead, saying developing countries are disadvantaged in the process and that some of its assumptions favour richer nations.

segments.title: A dispute about evidence and equity
segments.body:
Potsdam Institute director Johan Rockström says the assessment is an objective synthesis of peer-reviewed research and should not be delayed. Other developing countries, including small island states and least-developed countries, have also called for the work to proceed. The IPCC says 51% of the 664 appointed authors for its three reports come from developing countries and economies in transition.

Lidy Nacpil of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development argues that some emissions-cutting scenarios are biased against the global south, including by assuming that reductions should be made where they are cheapest. The disagreement remains unresolved as the IPCC faces a decision on its budget; without one, completing the reports before the stocktake could be difficult.

content.headline: A string of US outages exposes fragile systems and fuels cyber fears
content.shortHeadline: US outages expose fragile systems and fuel cyber fears
content.standfirst: Recent disruptions to aviation, software, banking and government networks have prompted fears of a coordinated attack, but reporting points to separate technical failures. Experts say ageing infrastructure and a faster pace of vulnerability discovery leave systems under strain.

sources.originalTitle: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?

segments.body: A faulty router replacement caused a nationwide US aviation communications failure that cancelled more than 18,000 flights. Other recent disruptions had different causes: a software bug affected Microsoft services, an Apple update caused app outages, and routine maintenance disrupted an internal NSA network. The reporting does not establish that the incidents were connected.

segments.title: Old infrastructure, new pressures
segments.body:
Experts point to ageing systems and the difficulty of replacing them, alongside pressure to patch software flaws found at increasing speed. Some vulnerabilities have been uncovered with AI tools, but the article notes that not all of the bugs are useful to attackers, and that the outages described had separate explanations.

The clustering of incidents has helped conspiracy claims spread online. A cognitive psychologist quoted in the report says transparent, accurate public communication can help counter those explanations. The larger concern is resilience: a single failure should not be able to bring a nationwide system to a halt.

content.headline: Reported hacks hit FBI crime database and US agriculture payment system
content.shortHeadline: FBI and agriculture systems reportedly hacked
content.standfirst: Reports say intruders accessed the FBI’s law-enforcement information network and a US agriculture department payment system. The extent of either breach remains unclear, and officials have not established a link to recent service outages.

sources.originalTitle: The FBI and USDA were reportedly hacked

segments.body: The FBI’s National Crime Information Center, used by federal, state and local law enforcement to share information including warrants and missing-person records, was reportedly hacked. The US Department of Agriculture’s payment platform was also reported compromised. The scope of the intrusions is not yet clear.

Former officials cited in reporting on the agriculture breach warned that access to the payment database might provide a route to more sensitive information, including food-safety data and research on animal-borne illness. The reports come amid other US service disruptions, but the supplied reporting does not show that these breaches caused those outages.

content.headline: Congress party protesters enter Meta offices in India over suspended accounts
content.shortHeadline: India protest targets Meta over suspended accounts
content.standfirst: Members of India’s opposition Congress party protested at Meta’s Delhi offices, demanding the restoration of party leaders’ Instagram accounts. Two accounts were restored, but the party says many others remain restricted.

sources.originalTitle: Protesters storm Meta offices in India

segments.body: Members of the Congress party’s youth wing protested outside Meta’s Delhi offices on Friday and appeared to enter the building in video shared by CNN. They want the company to restore accounts belonging to party leaders and have warned of further protests. Two of the accounts in question were restored that day.

The party accuses Meta of censoring speech opposed by Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his BJP party. Manu Jain, who oversees social media for the Congress youth wing, said thousands of accounts belonging to journalists, creators and government critics remain restricted. Meta had not responded to the report’s request for comment.

content.headline: An off-Broadway play uses Bluetooth broadcasts to tell a story about hearing
content.shortHeadline: Bluetooth audio turns a play into an experience of hearing loss
content.standfirst: In Love Me, audience headphones carry a character’s clear inner voice while theatre speakers reproduce muffled sound. The Auracast broadcast also supports hearing aids and cochlear implants, making the technology part of both the access and the storytelling.

sources.originalTitle: ‘The show is starting soon. Please turn on your headphones.’

segments.body: The off-Broadway production Love Me gives audience members headphones linked to an Auracast Bluetooth broadcast. The sound design shifts between the speakers in the theatre and audio in the headphones, including a clear inner monologue against muffled external sound, to help convey the central character’s experience of hearing loss.

The production also offers a broadcast intended for compatible hearing aids and cochlear implants, and provides captioned iPads. Auracast enables one audio stream to reach many nearby devices; here, it serves both as an accessibility tool and as part of the show’s form. The reporting describes the technology’s role in this production, not a general assessment of how it performs in other settings.

content.headline: Digital traces can comfort the bereaved, but AI recreations raise questions
content.shortHeadline: Digital memories bring comfort and new questions about grief
content.standfirst: Messages, photos and online memorials can help people stay connected to someone they have lost, while unexpected reminders or AI-generated versions may make grief harder for some. There is no single right way to manage a digital legacy.

image.caption: Kate Woodthorpe, who says digital legacies are likely to grow as more of life moves online.

sources.originalTitle: Are digital memories helping us or holding us back?

segments.body: Digital remnants of someone’s life can offer comfort or feel painful, depending on the person and how their grief changes. Bereavement specialist Karen Sutton advises people to notice whether reminders such as saved messages and phone notifications still help, and to change settings or remove them if they become distressing.

segments.title: What remains online
segments.body:
Sutton worries that AI-generated versions of people who have died could complicate bereavement by creating the impression that the person remains present. Researcher Kate Woodthorpe says the volume of digital material people leave behind is likely to grow as more of life takes place online.

Online spaces can also connect bereaved people: those interviewed describe finding community and support through social media and grief networks. Facebook and Instagram offer memorialised accounts, while some platforms allow families to request account removal.

content.headline: Two organisations say they verified an AI-assisted proof of the Riemann Hypoth
content.shortHeadline: Two groups verify Alpöge’s AI-assisted Riemann proof
content.standfirst: The Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative say they have independently checked Levent Alpöge’s formalised proof, developed with Claude. That is a major step in assessing the claim, though it is distinct from a prize decision or broad mathematical acceptance.

image.caption: Levent Alpöge, whose Lean proof of the Riemann hypothesis was reported as verified by two organisations.

sources.originalTitle: Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem
AI claimed a solution to the 167-year-old Riemann hypothesis — and a human did, too

segments.body: Two organisations working with the Lean proof language say they have verified Levent Alpöge’s proposed proof of the Riemann hypothesis. The Anthropic mathematician said Claude helped him develop the solution over about six weeks. The Lean Focused Research Organization and the Mathlib Initiative said they had full confidence that the proof is correct.

segments.title: What verification does—and does not—settle
segments.body: The result is a notable change from the initial uncertainty around Alpöge’s claim: the groups say the formalised Lean proof checks out. The supplied reporting does not say the Clay Mathematics Institute has awarded a prize or that the result has received general acceptance across mathematics. Making the argument understandable and assessing its wider significance remain part of the process.

perspectives.body: TechCrunch also reports a separate, human-only draft claiming the General Riemann hypothesis, attributed to Alessandro Masullo after 12 years’ work. That draft has not been formalised in Lean, and its correctness and status remain unestablished.

content.headline: Red Cross warns autonomous weapons may outpace efforts to set binding rules
content.shortHeadline: Red Cross warns autonomous weapons may outrun regulation
content.standfirst: After UN talks failed to establish a strong negotiating mandate, the International Committee of the Red Cross says autonomous weapons are advancing faster than regulation. Rights groups warn that delay leaves risks to civilians and the terms of use to militaries and industry.

image.caption: Delegates at the UN Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons meeting in Geneva.

sources.originalTitle: It will soon be too late to regulate use of autonomous weapons, warns Red Cross
International UN talks on controlling use of autonomous weapons collapse
The UN fails to agree on rules regulating ‘killer robots’

segments.body: The International Committee of the Red Cross and rights groups warn that the development and battlefield use of autonomous weapons may be outpacing international rules. At a week-long Geneva meeting of more than 120 states, efforts to agree a mandate for work on a legal instrument fell short of the urgent action advocates sought.

segments.title: A stalled process, disputed responsibility
segments.body: The Guardian reports that the need for consensus led the conference to adopt a weaker option: countries are to elaborate an instrument by consensus, which may not carry legal obligations. Its reporting describes Russia as leading objections and says the US and other military powers were also reluctant to commit to binding rules. More than 100 states had backed a new legal instrument.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s account highlights the consensus rule and the positions of several military powers, including US reluctance to accept a binding treaty. It also reports that a bloc of seven countries pushed for negotiations to begin within a year.

segments.title: Civilian harm and proposed limits
segments.body: The ICRC has called for prohibitions and restrictions, including a ban on using autonomous weapons against people and requirements that systems behave predictably and be limited to military objectives. The Guardian reports civilian deaths in Ukraine and describes concerns about AI-assisted target selection in Gaza and Iran; the supplied reports do not establish that every strike described was carried out by an autonomous weapon.

content.headline: Actor licenses his face for AI microdramas as creators weigh the risks
content.shortHeadline: Actor licenses his likeness for AI-made microdramas
content.standfirst: Aki Avni agreed to let a startup use his likeness in an AI-generated series, presenting a possible new source of work and income for performers. The company has not disclosed the deal’s terms, and critics worry automation could shrink opportunities for actors.

sources.originalTitle: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?

segments.body: Israeli actor Aki Avni licensed his likeness to Shortical for Inevitable, an AI-generated microdrama in which a digital version of him plays a fictionalised version of himself. Avni described the project as both exciting and nerve-racking. Shortical says this is its first use of a real person’s likeness and that it hopes the project will draw attention to face licensing.

segments.title: Consent, pay and work
segments.body:
Shortical advertises that people can submit their social-media profiles for possible licensing deals, but says the offer is in its early stages and has not yet led to other signed contracts. The company did not disclose Avni’s compensation or specific terms. Its representative said he was compensated at a level comparable to a non-AI acting role.

Consultant Jennifer Cooper says AI is already unsettling an industry that had offered work to emerging actors. The report also raises the prospect that likeness deals could tie compensation to audience engagement, but does not establish how that model will work in practice.

content.headline: South Korea’s education minister resigns after AI-assisted exam cheating
content.shortHeadline: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal
content.standfirst: A candidate used a concealed camera and smartphone to send exam questions to an AI system, prompting an emergency security overhaul before the national university entrance test. Education minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned, citing inadequate preparation.

image.caption: Students at a Seoul high school during South Korea’s university entrance exams.

sources.originalTitle: South Korean minister quits after AI cheating scandal engulfs university exams

segments.body: South Korea’s education minister, Choi Kyo-jin, resigned after a cheating scandal raised fears that AI could be used to gain an advantage in high-stakes exams. A top scorer in a national tax-accountancy test admitted using a miniature camera to photograph questions, sending them to an AI system and reading answers on a phone.

segments.title: Emergency controls
segments.body: Officials responded with extra supervisors, restrictions on what students could bring, checks for concealed devices and emergency phone alerts. Authorities identified 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices during the university entrance exam, nearly half through the alerts. Choi said he had failed to prepare adequately; the president accepted his resignation.

content.headline: Could AI lending models make credit decisions fairer—or repeat old biases?
content.shortHeadline: AI credit scoring promises inclusion but raises bias concerns
content.standfirst: Lenders are exploring machine-learning tools to assess applicants beyond conventional credit histories, which can leave some people overlooked. Experts warn that opaque models could also reproduce discrimination and make mistaken decisions harder to challenge.

sources.originalTitle: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?

segments.body: Credit scores can shape access to mortgages, loans and phone contracts, but they may not reflect a person’s current ability to repay. The report describes how identity fraud damaged one woman’s score and how a university student was denied a phone contract because she had too little credit history.

segments.title: More data, more accountability
segments.body:
Some lenders and credit firms are testing machine-learning systems that use wider sets of information. Supporters say this could help assess people with limited credit files. But Oxford professor Sandra Wachter warns that systems trained on historical decisions can reproduce social inequalities, while consumer advocates say people need to know what information is used and be able to challenge errors.

The report also describes a credit-reference startup that says it analyses transaction data without AI, citing concern that models could infer sensitive characteristics. The possible benefits of wider assessment remain in tension with privacy, transparency and bias risks.

content.headline: AI tools are making it easier to modify TVs, cameras and other gadgets
content.shortHeadline: AI tools bring device hacking to a wider audience
content.standfirst: Large language models can help users alter gadget software with prompts, extending a long-standing practice beyond experienced developers. The changes may unlock useful features, but can also break devices and leave users outside manufacturer support.

sources.originalTitle: The vibe-coding revolution is coming to all the gadgets

segments.body: A developer used Claude Code to remove unwanted software and redesign the interface on an Android TV. The project drew wide interest and reflects a broader trend: people are using language models to modify camera firmware, music devices and game consoles. The underlying techniques are not all new, but AI tools can make them easier to attempt.

segments.title: New access, new risks
segments.body:
Some manufacturers are embracing custom firmware or open-source tools, while others may respond with tighter controls, digital-rights restrictions or legal action. Modifying a device can also create security and reliability risks; users may have to rely on the same AI tools that made the changes to fix problems.

The developer behind CleanYourTV recommends backing up software and testing in a separate environment. The advice is practical rather than a guarantee: device updates and model changes can still produce problems.
